question.text:
\[ \begin{cases} x'(t) = 9y(t) \\[5pt] y'(t) = 9x(t) \end{cases} \] Which of the following gives the general solution to the system of ODEs above?

Hint: $e^{At} = \begin{bmatrix} \cosh(9t) & \sinh(9t) \\ \sinh(9t) & \cosh(9t) \end{bmatrix},$ where $A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 9 \\ 9 & 0 \end{bmatrix}.$
question.explanation:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get \[ \mathbf{x}'(t) = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 9 \\ 9 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{x}(t), \] where $\mathbf{x}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} x(t) \\ y(t) \end{bmatrix}.$ So, the matrix of the system is $A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 9 \\ 9 & 0 \end{bmatrix}.$

Given the system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as \[ \mathbf{x}(t) = \Phi(t) \, \mathbf{c}, \] where $\Phi(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $\mathbf{c}$ is a constant vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix $\Phi_0(t)$ of the system is given by \[ \Phi_0(t) = e^{At} = \begin{bmatrix} \cosh(9t) & \sinh(9t) \\ \sinh(9t) & \cosh(9t) \end{bmatrix}. \]

Therefore, the general solution is

\begin{align*} \mathbf{x}(t) &=\Phi_0(t) \, \mathbf{c} \\[5pt] &= e^{At} \, \mathbf{c} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} \cosh(9t) & \sinh(9t) \\ \sinh(9t) & \cosh(9t) \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} c_1 \\ c_2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= c_1\begin{bmatrix} \cosh(9t) \\ \sinh(9t) \end{bmatrix} + c_2\begin{bmatrix} \sinh(9t) \\ \cosh(9t) \end{bmatrix}, \end{align*}

where $c_1,c_2 \in \mathbb{R}.$

question.text:
\[ \begin{cases} x'(t) = 5y(t) \\[5pt] y'(t) = 5x(t), \end{cases} \qquad \begin{bmatrix} x(0) \\ y(0) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \] Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

Hint: $e^{At} = \begin{bmatrix} \cosh(5t) & \sinh(5t) \\ \sinh(5t) & \cosh(5t) \end{bmatrix},$ where $A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 5 \\ 5 & 0 \end{bmatrix}.$
question.explanation:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get \[ \mathbf{x}'(t) = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 5 \\ 5 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{x}(t), \] where $\mathbf{x}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} x(t) \\ y(t) \end{bmatrix}.$ So, the matrix of the system is $A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 5 \\ 5 & 0 \end{bmatrix}.$

Given the system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as \[ \mathbf{x}(t) = \Phi_0(t) \, \mathbf{x}(0), \] where $\Phi_0(t) = e^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system, and $\mathbf{x}(0)$ is the initial condition vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix $\Phi_0(t)$ of the system is given by

\[ \Phi_0(t) = e^{At} = \begin{bmatrix} \cosh(5t) & \sinh(5t) \\ \sinh(5t) & \cosh(5t) \end{bmatrix}. \]

Therefore, the solution is

\begin{align*} \mathbf{x}(t) &= e^{At} \, \mathbf{x}(0) \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} \cosh(5t) & \sinh(5t) \\ \sinh(5t) & \cosh(5t) \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -2\cosh(5t) \\ -2\sinh(5t)\end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

question.freeAnswerChoice:

[answer: 2\sin(3(t-2)); type: expression; width: 120; margin-left: 4; margin-right: 4; buttons: frac, cos, sin, exp;]
question.explanation:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get \[ \mathbf{x}'(t) = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -3 \\ 3 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{x}(t), \] where $\mathbf{x}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} x(t) \\ y(t) \end{bmatrix}.$ So, the matrix of the system is $A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -3 \\ 3 & 0 \end{bmatrix}.$

Given the system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as \[ \mathbf{x}(t) = \Phi(t) \, \mathbf{c}, \] where $\Phi(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $\mathbf{c}$ is a constant vector.

So, we can write our general solution as \[ \mathbf{x}(t) = \Phi_0(t) \mathbf{c} =e^{At} \, \mathbf{c}, \] where $\Phi_0(t) = e^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system. Substituting $t=t_0,$ we have \[ \mathbf{x}(t_0) = e^{At_0} \, \mathbf{c}, \] and since $e^{At}$ is invertible for all $t,$ we have \[ \mathbf{c} = e^{-At_0} \, \mathbf{x}(t_0). \]

Plugging the above back into our expression for $\mathbf{x}(t),$ we get \begin{align*} \mathbf{x}(t) &= e^{At} \, e^{-At_0} \, \mathbf{x}(t_0) \\[5pt] &= e^{A(t-t_0)} \, \mathbf{x}(t_0). \end{align*}

Therefore, the solution is \begin{align*} \mathbf{x}(t) &= e^{A(t-2)} \, \mathbf{x}(2) \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} \cos(3(t-2)) & -\sin(3(t-2)) \\ \sin(3(t-2)) & \cos(3(t-2)) \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} \hspace{2pt}\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt lightgray]{2\cos(3(t-2))} \hspace{2pt}\\ \hspace{2pt}\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt lightgray]{2\sin(3(t-2))} \hspace{2pt} \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

question.text:
\[ \begin{cases} x'(t) = -4y(t) \\[5pt] y'(t) = -4x(t), \end{cases} \qquad \begin{bmatrix} x(1) \\ y(1) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix} \] Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

Hint: $e^{At} = \begin{bmatrix} \cosh(4t) & -\sinh(4t) \\ -\sinh(4t) & \cosh(4t) \end{bmatrix},$ where $A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -4 \\ -4 & 0 \end{bmatrix}.$
question.explanation:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get \[ \mathbf{x}'(t) = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -4 \\ -4 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{x}(t), \] where $\mathbf{x}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} x(t) \\ y(t) \end{bmatrix}.$ So, the matrix of the system is $A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -4 \\ -4 & 0 \end{bmatrix}.$

Given the system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as \[ \mathbf{x}(t) = \Phi(t) \, \mathbf{c}, \] where $\Phi(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $\mathbf{c}$ is a constant vector.

So, we can write our general solution as \[ \mathbf{x}(t) = \Phi_0(t) \mathbf{c} = e^{At} \, \mathbf{c}, \] where $\Phi_0(t) = e^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system. Substituting $t = t_0,$ we have \[ \mathbf{x}(t_0) = e^{At_0} \, \mathbf{c}, \] and since $e^{At}$ is invertible for all $t,$ we have \[ \mathbf{c} = e^{-At_0} \, \mathbf{x}(t_0). \]

Plugging the above back into our expression for $\mathbf{x}(t),$ we get \begin{align*} \mathbf{x}(t) &= e^{At} \, e^{-At_0} \, \mathbf{x}(t_0) \\[5pt] &= e^{A(t-t_0)} \, \mathbf{x}(t_0). \end{align*}

Therefore, the solution is \begin{align*} \mathbf{x}(t) &= e^{A(t-1)} \, \mathbf{x}(1) \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} \cosh(4(t-1)) & -\sinh(4(t-1)) \\ -\sinh(4(t-1)) & \cosh(4(t-1)) \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 2\sinh(4(t-1)) \\ -2\cosh(4(t-1)) \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

question.text:
Consider the homogeneous system $\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. You're given that the standard fundamental matrix $\Phi_0(t)$ is the unique solution to the initial value problem \[ \Phi_0'(t) = A\Phi_0(t), \qquad \Phi_0(0) = I_n. \] A derivation of the formula for the solution $\mathbf{x}(t)$ passing through $\mathbf{x}(0)$ is presented below.

$\textrm{L1}{:}\;$ Let $\Phi_0(t)=e^{At}$

$\textrm{L2}{:}\;$ $\mathbf{x}(t)=\Phi_0(t)\,\mathbf{c}$ for some constant vector $\mathbf{c}$

$\textrm{L3}{:}\;$ $\mathbf{x}(0)=\Phi_0(0) \, \mathbf{c}$

$\textrm{L4}{:}\;$ $\Phi_0(0)=I_n$

$\textrm{L5}{:}\;$ $\mathbf{x}(0)=\mathbf{c}$

$\textrm{L6}{:}\;$ $\mathbf{x}(t)=e^{At} \, \mathbf{x}(0)$

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.
question.explanation:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

  • We first consider lines $\textrm{L2}$ and $\textrm{L3}.$ Starting from $\textrm{L2},$ we have the identity \[ \mathbf{x}(t)=\Phi_0(t)\,\mathbf{c}. \] Evaluating this identity at $t=0$ gives \[ \mathbf{x}(0)=\Phi_0(0)\mathbf{c}, \] which is exactly line $\textrm{L3}.$ Therefore, $\textrm{L3}$ follows from $\textrm{L2}$ by $\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt lightgray]{\text{evaluating both sides at $t=0$}}.$

  • Next, we consider lines $\textrm{L3}$, $\textrm{L4},$ and $\textrm{L5}.$ From $\textrm{L3}$ we have \[ \mathbf{x}(0)=\Phi_0(0)\mathbf{c}, \] and from $\textrm{L4}$ we know $\Phi_0(0)=I_n.$ Substituting $\Phi_0(0)=I_n$ into $\mathbf{x}(0)=\Phi_0(0)\mathbf{c}$ gives \[ \mathbf{x}(0)=I_n\mathbf{c}=\mathbf{c}, \] which is exactly line $\textrm{L5}.$ Thus, $\textrm{L5}$ follows from lines $\textrm{L3}$ and $\textrm{L4}$ by $\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt lightgray]{\text{substituting $\Phi_0(0)=I_n$ into $\mathbf{x}(0)=\Phi_0(0)\mathbf{c}$}}.$

  • Finally, we consider lines $\textrm{L1}$, $\textrm{L2},$ $\textrm{L5},$ and $\textrm{L6}.$ From $\textrm{L1}$ we have $\Phi_0(t)=e^{At},$ and from $\textrm{L5}$ we know $\mathbf{c}=\mathbf{x}(0).$ Substituting $\Phi_0(t)=e^{At}$ from $\textrm{L1}$ and $\mathbf{c}=\mathbf{x}(0)$ from $\textrm{L5}$ into $\mathbf{x}(t)=\Phi_0(t)\,\mathbf{c}$ (line $\textrm{L2}$), we obtain \[ \mathbf{x}(t)=e^{At}\,\mathbf{x}(0). \] Thus, $\textrm{L6}$ follows from $\textrm{L2}$ and substitution from $\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt lightgray]{\text{$\textrm{L1}$ and $\textrm{L5}$}}.$
